analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal crop insurance subsidies for the largest farms and caps what private insurance companies can earn running the program.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in November 2015, received no further action, and never became law before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government pays most of the premium for the crop insurance policies that farms buy from private insurance companies. This bill would cut back that subsidy for the largest operations, put an overall dollar cap on what the private insurance companies can bill the government for running the program, cap their profit rate, allow the government to renegotiate its deal with those companies to save money, and make public the names of who receives the subsidies and how much. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, and small and mid-sized farmers who compete against large operations. The bill trims subsidies that flow disproportionately to the biggest farming entities and reduces the guaranteed profits of the private insurance companies that administer the program. Families who pay taxes to fund the program would bear less of the cost of insuring the largest farms.

how_it_helps.text: Ends federal premium subsidies for crop insurance beyond basic coverage for any person or entity with adjusted gross income over $250,000, and caps subsidies at $40,000 per person per year.
Caps total administrative and operating reimbursements to crop insurance companies at $900 million (rising with inflation) and caps their overall rate of return at 8.9% of retained premium.
Lets USDA renegotiate its agreement with private insurers without a budget-neutrality requirement, opening the door to savings, and bars subsidies for harvest-price revenue policies.
Requires USDA to publish annually the names of subsidy recipients and amounts, plus each private insurer's underwriting gains and federal payments.

analysis.who_pays: The largest farming operations and wealthy investors in farmland, who would lose federal premium subsidies above $40,000 a year and lose them entirely for added coverage if their income exceeds $250,000. Private crop insurance companies would also see their administrative reimbursements and profits capped.

drawbacks.text: Some large farming operations would have lost part of their federally subsidized insurance coverage, which defenders of the program argue helps manage genuine weather and price risks in agriculture.

Capping insurers' rate of return and administrative reimbursements could reduce the private insurance companies' incentive to participate in the program, a concern the industry could raise against the redesign.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were real but targeted: ending premium subsidies for large agribusiness entities and capping the private companies' guaranteed returns would have cut federal spending with little effect on typical family farms. The honest cost is that some large farming operations would have paid more for crop insurance, and the insurance companies argued tighter margins could reduce their willingness to participate in the program. On balance, the design aimed reform at the largest beneficiaries rather than at the program itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on introduction and never received a vote or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on November 5, 2015 and read twice.
It was referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took up no further action on it.
No vote was ever held, no committee markup occurred, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crop insurance companies and the largest farming operations were better off, because the subsidies and guaranteed returns the bill would have trimmed were left in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crop insurers and the largest farms

for.name: Sen. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Agriculture Committee.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral, never scheduling a markup or vote, which ended the bill when the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but with no votes taken there is no record of where the parties stood as a whole.

industries.note: The bill caps their administrative reimbursements at $900 million a year and caps their rate of return at 8.9%, cutting a guaranteed federal revenue stream. It would also require public disclosure of their gains, but would leave the industry running the program.

Farms with adjusted gross income over $250,000 would lose subsidies for additional coverage, and no single entity could receive more than $40,000 a year in premium subsidies. Small and mid-sized farms would keep their subsidies largely unchanged.
The bill reduces federal spending on crop insurance, one of the largest agriculture subsidies, by limiting payments that currently flow mostly to large operations and private insurers.
